JSON: Name: model_guided_dl_chaos_detection Title: Model-guided deep learning ensemble for detecting chaotic versus regular dynamics in short noisy biological time series Short Hypothesis: An ensemble of LSTM classifiers trained on generic chaotic map data and selected by performance on a domain-specific APD heart-map will classify short noisy cardiac APD time series as chaotic or regular with at least 90% overall accuracy on held-out ex-vivo frog heart recordings. Related Work: Classical methods for chaos detection (Lyapunov exponent estimation, permutation entropy, and the 0-1 test) provide interpretable diagnostics but require long, low-noise time series and become unreliable on short noisy biological recordings. Machine learning and deep learning approaches have been applied to detect or predict chaotic dynamics, but prior DL methods typically require large in-domain training datasets, multi-variable recordings, or direct training on simulated models matching the target system; this limits their applicability when experimental data are short, noisy, and scarce. Reservoir computing and recurrent architectures can forecast or reproduce chaotic attractors but often do not provide robust binary chaos/regular labels for short traces and lack automated model-guided network selection. Existing approaches therefore suffer from (1) sensitivity to short trace length and observational noise, (2) dependence on in-domain training data that may be unavailable, (3) lack of principled network-selection criteria tied to domain-specific simulated dynamics, and (4) limited evaluation on real biological datasets with realistic class imbalance and labeling ambiguity. Abstract: We address automated detection of chaotic versus regular dynamics in short, noisy biological time series by combining generic deep-learning training and model-guided network selection. The method trains multiple recurrent neural networks (stacked LSTMs) on synthetic data from a canonical chaotic map to capture generic temporal signatures of regular and chaotic regimes. Candidate networks are then evaluated and selected using simulated output from a domain-specific one-dimensional cardiac APD restitution map (with controlled noise levels), producing a robustness-ranked ensemble member for deployment. The selected network is applied to ex-vivo frog cardiac APD recordings of variable length and noise. The main contribution is a reproducible pipeline that decouples universal chaotic-feature learning from domain-specific selection, enabling reliable classification when experimental traces are too short for classical chaos measures. We expect the pipeline to yield high classification accuracy and noise robustness on real cardiac recordings while maintaining a scalable procedure for other biological time-series domains where in-domain training data are limited. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Synthetic training: logistic map dataset with 2,000 regular and 2,000 chaotic time series, each length 1000, additional validation and test sets drawn from different initial conditions; (2) Simulated selection: Beeler–Reuter APD heart-map BCL-parametric sweep producing 12,000 simulated time series, each generated for 20,500 timesteps with last 1000 retained; additive Gaussian noise levels mu in {0.0, 0.5, 1.0} applied and repeated 100 trials per noise level; (3) Real experimental: Frog heart APD Dataset1 (52 traces, length range 15–205) and Dataset2 (24 traces, length range 21–521) with expert labels. Baselines: permutation entropy classifier (fixed parameters n=3, tau=1); 0-1 test for chaos; direct Lyapunov exponent estimation when applicable; LSTM trained directly on simulated APD heart-map data; reservoir computing classifier; MLP classifier trained on same features. Model and training: stacked two-layer unidirectional LSTM (hidden size 4 per layer), linear 2-way softmax output; cross-entropy loss with L2 weight decay 1e-5; Adam optimizer lr=0.008; batch size 32; up to 2000 epochs with early stopping on validation loss; train 10 random initializations. Selection procedure: evaluate each trained network on noisy Beeler–Reuter simulated sets and compute mean±std of Accuracy, Accuracy_chaotic (sensitivity), Accuracy_regular (specificity), Accuracy_EPs, Accuracy_POs and robustness diff = 100 * |S(mu=0) ∩ S(mu)| / |S(mu)| as in algorithm; select network(s) satisfying thresholds (mean accuracies >75% and diff<1%, std<1%). Evaluation metrics: overall accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score for chaotic class, area under ROC, confusion matrices, mean±std across repeats, calibration of softmax scores, and robustness diff at each mu. Experimental setup: normalize inputs to [0,1] prior to inference; evaluate selected networks on frog datasets producing per-trace softmax scores; repeat selection and inference 100 times with different random seeds to estimate variability. Ablation studies: (A) training data source: logistic-only vs logistic+APD simulated augmentation; (B) architecture variants: stacked LSTM vs single LSTM vs GRU vs BiLSTM vs reservoir; (C) input length sensitivity: evaluate with truncated lengths {50,100,250,500,1000}; (D) selection criteria sensitivity: vary thresholds for mean accuracy and diff; (E) noise robustness: evaluate at mu in {0,0.5,1.0} and compute diff metric. Statistical analysis: report paired comparisons between proposed method and each baseline using McNemar's test and paired t-tests on per-trace accuracies; report mean±95% CI. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: trained LSTMs may overfit generic-map features that do not transfer to the target biological system if the model-guided selection fails due to model mismatch; selected network outputs may be poorly calibrated and produce ambiguous softmax scores near 0.5 for borderline traces. Data and evaluation biases: expert labels on experimental traces are subjective for near-boundary or transient-rich series and introduce label noise; class imbalance (few chaotic samples) may inflate apparent performance for majority class and reduce statistical power to evaluate chaotic-class sensitivity. Scalability and compute: training multiple LSTMs and repeated selection runs across noise trials increases compute cost and may be prohibitive for large-scale deployment. Limits to generalization: approach depends on the availability of a domain-specific mathematical model of similar dynamical nature; when such a model is unavailable or incorrect, network selection may be invalid. Short/noisy traces: for extremely short recordings (<<50 points) or very high observational noise, neither the DL classifier nor baselines can reliably distinguish regimes; classical Lyapunov estimation remains infeasible. Hyperparameter sensitivity: results depend on architecture, selection thresholds, normalization, and random seeds, causing reproducibility risk if not fully specified.
